title: Golden Trump Statue Appears at CPAC 2021
description_medium: A gold-colored statue of Donald Trump appeared at the Conservative Political Action Conference in Orlando, Florida, in February 2021. Sculptor Tommy Zegan created the more-than-six-foot fiberglass figure, which showed Trump wearing an American-flag-patterned outfit and holding a miniature wand. Visitors photographed the statue as it was moved through the convention venue. Its display became a widely circulated image from CPAC, though political interpretations of the object varied among attendees and commentators.
description_long: The gold-colored Trump statue was displayed during the Conservative Political Action Conference in Orlando on February 25–28, 2021, shortly after Trump had left the presidency. Created by sculptor Tommy Zegan, the figure stood more than six feet tall and depicted Trump in a suit patterned with the American flag, carrying a wand topped with an eagle. Video of the statue being wheeled through the hotel circulated widely online, and attendees stopped to pose with it. Zegan said he intended the statue as a tribute to Trump; other observers treated it as a symbol of the former president’s continued influence over Republican politics. These are interpretations of the image, rather than an official CPAC statement or evidence of how all participants viewed it. The object also drew coverage about its materials and production, including reports that components were made in China and that it was assembled in Mexico. Its unusual appearance at the conference made it a visual emblem of the 2021 gathering, where Trump’s allies debated the direction of the Republican Party after the 2020 election. The statue’s display documents that political moment without requiring a generalized claim that it represented every conservative attendee’s beliefs.
evidence_notes: Guardian identifies sculptor and production; Washington Post dates CPAC display. “Symbol” interpretations are attributed, not treated as universal attendee views.
corrected_wording: Proposed correction: Golden Trump Statue Appears at CPAC 2021. See evidence_notes for scope and evidence qualification.

title: Trump Announces U.S. Withdrawal from Paris Climate Agreement
description_medium: On June 1, 2017, President Donald Trump announced that the United States would withdraw from the Paris climate agreement and seek either a revised arrangement or a new deal. The announcement changed federal policy but did not make withdrawal immediate: the agreement’s rules delayed formal notice until November 2019, and the exit took effect in November 2020. The United States rejoined in 2021 under President Joe Biden. Trump ordered a second withdrawal process in 2025, a separate action.
description_long: Trump announced the decision to leave the Paris Agreement at the White House on June 1, 2017, saying the deal imposed unfair economic burdens and that his administration would seek better terms. The agreement is an international framework under which participating countries submit climate commitments and report progress; it does not set a uniform emissions quota enforced by a global authority. Because of the agreement’s withdrawal clause, the United States could not formally submit notice until three years after it entered into force, and withdrawal would take another year to become effective. The Trump administration submitted notice in November 2019, making the exit effective on November 4, 2020. President Biden rejoined in January 2021. Trump’s January 2025 executive order initiated a new withdrawal, distinct from the first-term announcement and completed exit. The announcement signaled a policy reversal in U.S. climate diplomacy, while the legal withdrawal took effect more than three years later. The 2025 order initiated another withdrawal, distinct from the first-term process.
evidence_notes: Archived White House page dates the announcement; State Department explains formal notice/effective timeline. The 2025 order is a separate withdrawal process.
corrected_wording: Proposed correction: Trump Announces U.S. Withdrawal from Paris Climate Agreement. See evidence_notes for scope and evidence qualification.

title: Trump Retweets Anti-Muslim Videos from Britain First
description_medium: On November 29, 2017, President Donald Trump retweeted three videos posted by Jayda Fransen, deputy leader of the British far-right group Britain First. The clips were presented with anti-Muslim captions, and at least one caption was disputed by Dutch authorities. The retweets amplified a fringe group’s content from the president’s account and drew criticism in the United States and Britain. The White House defended Trump’s decision, while British Prime Minister Theresa May said it was wrong to do so.
description_long: Trump’s personal Twitter account shared three videos originally posted by Jayda Fransen, then deputy leader of Britain First, on November 29, 2017. The group campaigned against Islam and immigration and was described by contemporary reporting as far right. Fransen’s captions presented the clips as examples of violence involving Muslims. One video’s description was challenged by the Dutch embassy, which said its caption was false; the clips’ provenance and the events depicted were not consistently established by the posts themselves. The retweets were visible to Trump’s large audience and quickly prompted criticism from British political leaders, including Prime Minister Theresa May, who said the president was wrong to amplify the material. The White House initially defended the sharing, saying it did not matter whether the videos were authentic if they depicted threats. Trump later said he had retweeted them because he believed they raised security concerns. The episode was notable because the president’s account gave international visibility to a small extremist group and its inflammatory content. Describing that amplification does not establish that Trump verified the clips or endorsed every claim in their captions.
evidence_notes: PBS and contemporaneous reporting identify Fransen, three retweets and political response. Captions and video authenticity varied; qualify disputed content.
corrected_wording: Proposed correction: Trump Retweets Anti-Muslim Videos from Britain First. See evidence_notes for scope and evidence qualification.

title: Trump Threatens to Sue Ted Cruz Over Canadian Birth
description_medium: During the 2016 Republican presidential primary, Donald Trump threatened to sue rival Ted Cruz over whether Cruz’s birth in Calgary, Canada, made him eligible to serve as president. Cruz was born to an American mother and argued that he was a natural-born citizen. Trump raised the issue before South Carolina’s February 20 primary and suggested that litigation could follow if Cruz won the nomination. No court decided the dispute because Trump did not file the threatened suit.
description_long: Trump challenged Cruz’s constitutional eligibility as the two competed for the 2016 Republican nomination. Cruz was born in Calgary in 1970 to an American mother and a Cuban father, and had lived in Texas for decades. The Constitution requires a president to be a “natural born Citizen,” but courts had not definitively resolved every scenario involving a candidate born abroad to a U.S. citizen parent. On February 15, 2016, Trump told reporters in South Carolina that he might file a lawsuit if Cruz secured the nomination, arguing that the question could create a problem for the party in the general election. Cruz called the attack a political tactic and maintained that he qualified. Legal scholars disagreed about the unsettled contours of the phrase, though many concluded that a person born abroad to a U.S.-citizen parent met the requirement. Trump never brought the threatened case, and the Republican nomination contest ended when Cruz suspended his campaign in May 2016. The episode illustrates how the eligibility question became a primary-campaign dispute; it did not produce a judicial ruling on Cruz’s status. The National Archives Constitution transcript supplies the constitutional text but not evidence of Trump’s threat or its campaign context.
evidence_notes: Washington Post dates and contextualizes the threat. Constitution is primary context only; no lawsuit or judicial determination followed.
corrected_wording: Proposed correction: Trump Threatens to Sue Ted Cruz Over Canadian Birth. See evidence_notes for scope and evidence qualification.

title: Trump Administration Withdraws U.S. from U.N. Human Rights Council
description_medium: On June 19, 2018, U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Nikki Haley and Secretary of State Mike Pompeo announced that the United States would withdraw from the U.N. Human Rights Council. They criticized the council’s treatment of Israel and its membership of states with poor human-rights records, while arguing that reform efforts had failed. The decision ended U.S. participation before its elected term expired. The administration later rejoined the council in 2021 under President Biden.
description_long: Haley and Pompeo announced the U.S. withdrawal from the U.N. Human Rights Council at the State Department on June 19, 2018. The council is a United Nations body that reviews the human-rights records of member states and adopts resolutions and recommendations. Haley criticized what she described as persistent bias against Israel and objected to the council’s membership of governments accused of serious abuses. She said the United States had sought reforms but would not remain a member if the body continued to operate as she described. Critics, including human-rights organizations and U.N. officials, argued that leaving surrendered a seat and reduced U.S. influence over investigations and debate. The withdrawal did not dissolve the council or prevent the United States from engaging with it as an observer, but it ended U.S. membership during the remainder of the term. President Biden’s administration announced a return in 2021 and later secured election to a new term. The episode was thus a withdrawal from a multilateral oversight forum followed by a later policy reversal. It should be distinguished from the separate question of whether the council’s performance warranted reform.
evidence_notes: State Department statement confirms date and administration’s rationale. Include later 2021 return as outcome; criticism of the body is attributed.
corrected_wording: Proposed correction: Trump Administration Withdraws U.S. from U.N. Human Rights Council. See evidence_notes for scope and evidence qualification.

title: Trump Says Revolutionary War Army Took Over Airports
description_medium: During his July 4, 2019, “Salute to America” speech, President Trump said the Continental Army “took over the airports” while describing the Revolutionary War. Airports did not exist in the eighteenth century, and the line was widely treated as a historical gaffe. The transcript shows he also referred to Fort McHenry, a site of the War of 1812, within the same passage about the Revolutionary War. The remark drew public ridicule but did not involve a policy announcement.
description_long: Trump delivered the “Salute to America” address at the Lincoln Memorial on July 4, 2019. In a passage praising the Continental Army, he said it “manned the air” and “took over the airports,” language that appeared to confuse historical periods: powered aircraft and airports were developed more than a century after the Revolutionary War. In the same passage he referred to Fort McHenry and the “rockets’ red glare,” imagery associated with the War of 1812 and the national anthem rather than the Revolutionary War. The speech was part of a large Independence Day event featuring military equipment and performances. The airports line quickly became a subject of jokes and political commentary, with supporters and critics debating whether it was a verbal stumble or a scripted error. The transcript supports the quotation and context; it does not resolve how the mistake occurred. The airports line was a historical misstatement during a ceremonial address; it was not a policy announcement.
evidence_notes: Transcript supports wording; Fort McHenry reference concerns 1814. The description calls it a gaffe without asserting intent.
corrected_wording: Proposed correction: Trump Says Revolutionary War Army Took Over Airports. See evidence_notes for scope and evidence qualification.

title: Trump Fires 17 Inspectors General Without 30-Day Notice
description_medium: On January 24, 2025, President Trump dismissed about 17 inspectors general across federal agencies. The firings included watchdogs at departments such as Defense, State and Transportation. Federal law requires advance notice to Congress and a detailed explanation before an inspector general is removed; the White House did not provide the required 30-day notice at the time. The action prompted bipartisan criticism and legal scrutiny because inspectors general conduct independent audits and investigations within the executive branch.
description_long: Trump removed approximately 17 inspectors general late on January 24, 2025, in an unusually broad action affecting independent watchdog offices across the federal government. Inspectors general audit agency spending, investigate misconduct and report findings to agency leaders and Congress. A 2022 amendment to the Inspector General Act requires the president to give Congress 30 days’ advance notice of a removal and provide a substantive rationale. The White House sent termination notices but did not provide that advance notice before the dismissals. Republican Senator Chuck Grassley, chair of the Senate Judiciary Committee, said the administration had not supplied the detailed notice required by law and called for further information. The administration argued that the president had authority to remove executive officials. The episode raised concerns about the independence of oversight while the administration began major policy and staffing changes. The number of inspectors general affected and notice requirement are matters separate from whether every individual removal was later found unlawful; courts and Congress examined different legal issues in subsequent proceedings. The event should therefore be described as a mass dismissal that bypassed the statutory notice period, followed by disputes about the administration’s authority and compliance.
evidence_notes: AP reports about 17 removals and quotes Grassley on statutory notice; statute amended in 2022 establishes 30-day advance notice. “Unlawful” not asserted as a final adjudication.
corrected_wording: Proposed correction: Trump Fires 17 Inspectors General Without 30-Day Notice. See evidence_notes for scope and evidence qualification.

title: Trump Management Settles Federal Housing Discrimination Case
description_medium: In 1973, the Justice Department sued Fred Trump, Donald Trump and Trump Management, alleging that the company discriminated against Black renters in its New York apartment buildings. The case ended in a June 1975 consent decree requiring nondiscrimination and an affirmative compliance program, including vacancy reporting and outreach to minority applicants. The settlement expressly was not an admission of liability. The Justice Department later raised compliance concerns, but the agreement itself did not constitute a court finding that the defendants had violated the Fair Housing Act.
description_long: The Justice Department filed a Fair Housing Act case in October 1973 against Fred Trump, Donald Trump and Trump Management, which operated apartment complexes in New York City. The complaint alleged that Black applicants were denied housing or treated differently when seeking apartments. The defendants contested the allegations. In June 1975, the parties entered a consent decree without a trial or admission of liability. It barred discrimination and required an affirmative compliance program, including written rental standards, notices that apartments were available without discrimination, and regular vacancy information for a civil-rights organization. The settlement thus imposed specific obligations while leaving the original allegations unadjudicated. In 1978, the Justice Department sent correspondence alleging that the company had not complied and raising new testing incidents; Trump Management disputed the department’s position. The 1975 agreement was binding but was not a judicial finding that the company had committed discrimination. Later disputes about compliance likewise need to be attributed to the parties unless established in court. The episode concerns federal enforcement of fair-housing rules in the Trump family’s rental business, not a criminal prosecution.
evidence_notes: Clearinghouse and decree support allegations, settlement date/terms and no-admission clause. Later compliance disputes are attributed, not described as proven violations or a 1978 second decree.
corrected_wording: Proposed correction: Trump Management Settles Federal Housing Discrimination Case. See evidence_notes for scope and evidence qualification.

title: Trump Mocks Reporter Serge Kovaleski’s Disability at Campaign Rally
description_medium: At a November 2015 campaign rally in South Carolina, Donald Trump imitated the movements of New York Times reporter Serge Kovaleski, who has arthrogryposis, a congenital condition affecting his joints. Trump was criticizing Kovaleski’s reporting about people celebrating after the September 11 attacks. Trump said he was mocking the reporter’s retracted description rather than his disability; Kovaleski said he did not recall Trump as having the physical mannerisms Trump acted out. The episode drew criticism and renewed attention to the underlying 2001 report.
description_long: Trump’s November 24, 2015, rally in Myrtle Beach, South Carolina, included a segment about a 2001 Washington Post report written by Serge Kovaleski, then a reporter at the paper. The article said authorities had detained and questioned people reportedly seen celebrating the September 11 attacks; it did not say thousands of Muslims celebrated across New Jersey, as Trump later claimed. While discussing the article, Trump made jerking arm movements and spoke in an exaggerated voice. Kovaleski has arthrogryposis, a congenital condition that limits movement in his arms. Trump denied mocking the reporter’s disability, saying he was imitating a person who had supposedly changed his account. Kovaleski said he did not remember Trump as having the physical mannerisms portrayed, and the Times defended its reporter. The footage and conflicting explanations became a major campaign controversy. The 2001 report’s wording was narrower than Trump’s later claim that large numbers of Muslims had celebrated the attacks. The incident occurred in a political argument about the story’s contents and became a separate controversy over how Trump represented a disabled journalist.
evidence_notes: Contemporaneous reporting and video document the gesture and competing explanations. Distinguish Trump’s broad claims about celebrations from the 2001 article’s narrower wording.
corrected_wording: Proposed correction: Trump Mocks Reporter Serge Kovaleski’s Disability at Campaign Rally. See evidence_notes for scope and evidence qualification.

title: New York Times Reports Trump Received $413 Million from His Father
description_medium: A 2018 New York Times investigation reported that Donald Trump received at least $413 million in today’s dollars from his father Fred Trump’s real-estate business over several decades. The report described loans, gifts and transfers, including property valuations and tax arrangements that tax experts questioned. The $413 million figure referred to Donald Trump, not a combined amount for him and his siblings. Trump’s lawyer denied that the family engaged in fraud or tax evasion; the Times said its investigation drew on more than 100,000 pages of financial records.
description_long: The New York Times published a year-long investigation on October 2, 2018, examining how Donald Trump accumulated wealth through his father Fred Trump’s real-estate empire. It reported that Donald Trump received at least $413 million in inflation-adjusted value over his lifetime, through a mix of loans, gifts, income and transfers. The investigation examined property valuations, family companies and tax filings, including transactions that experts said appeared to reduce estate and gift taxes. Tax specialists interviewed by the Times said some practices went beyond aggressive use of legal loopholes and appeared to involve fraud; that was expert analysis reported by the newspaper, not a criminal conviction. Trump’s attorney denied that there had been fraud or tax evasion and called the reporting inaccurate. The story challenged Trump’s repeated portrayal of himself as largely self-made from a modest loan, while showing that the figure did not describe money received by all his siblings together. New York State tax authorities said they were reviewing the report’s allegations. This entry records the investigation’s findings and attributed responses, rather than presenting disputed legal conclusions as adjudicated facts.
evidence_notes: NYT report and contemporary summaries support $413M in today’s dollars to Donald Trump and expert assessments; include Trump lawyer’s denial and distinguish allegations from adjudicated findings.
corrected_wording: Proposed correction: New York Times Reports Trump Received $413 Million from His Father. See evidence_notes for scope and evidence qualification.
